newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sees internal power struggles in Iraq.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sees internal power struggles in Iraq.

text.p: The White House on Wednesday said there are "internal struggles for power" in Iraq that suggest dissatisfaction with the regime of Saddam Hussein.

Reinforcing a report of apparent instability in Iraq circulated on Tuesday by a U.S. military source, White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry offered a terse but carefully worded assessment of the political situation in Baghdad.

"There are a great deal of complicated internal struggles for power" going on, McCurry said in response to questions on that earlier report, which suggested Saddam had put his own wife under house arrest and was changing locations more frequently out of apparent fear for his safety.
"There have been some things that have happened there recently ... (some) that have been reported publicly that would indicate some internal machinations," McCurry said.

A senior U.S. military officer summoned reporters to his Pentagon offices on Tuesday to say that various sources he considered reliable had reported signs of increasing trouble surrounding President Saddam, a bitter foe of the United States since U.S.-led forces ousted Iraqi invaders from Kuwait in the 1991 Gulf War.

Besides the reported house arrest of Saddam's wife, the U.S. officer, who asked not to be identified, said Saddam was now moving around even more frequently than he usually does in order to ensure his own safety.
He also said th Iraqi ruler's eldest son and heir apparent, Uday, might lose a leg to gangrene as a result of a Dec. 12 grenade and machine-gun attack in Baghdad.
Against that background, McCurry said on Wednesday that Washington was "closely monitoring" the situation in Iraq.
"The president (Bill Clinton) also has foremost on his mind the threats to regional security, particularly in the Persian Gulf," McCurry said.
He added, however, that there were no indications of troop movements that would suggest any renewed threat to Kuwait.

The Pentagon source had said that Saddam's military forces had increased their training in recent weeks, but he too said there was no indication Iraq might repeat its 1990 attack on Kuwait, which led to the Gulf War.
Saddam has been a thorn in the side of U.S. policymakers, who assumed the harsh economic sanctions imposed since the Gulf War would have long since undermined his ability to remain in power.
